articles.title: Walmart and Costco will shut their doors on Thanksgiving Day in the US before reopening on Black Friday; here is what shoppers need to know about holiday closures and the return of major retailers
articles.summary: Shoppers across the United States will have to plan their Thanksgiving purchases ahead of time as several major retailers prepare to close for the holiday
articles.body: Shoppers across the United States will have to plan their Thanksgiving purchases ahead of time as several major retailers prepare to close for the holiday on November 26, 2026. Walmart, Costco, Target and Best Buy are among the big names that will suspend in-store operations on Thursday before welcoming customers back for Black Friday shopping on November 27. According to the Associated Press (AP), ABC News and The Washington Post, the closures will affect not just retail stores but also banks, government offices and regular package delivery services. While most major chains will remain shut for the holiday, some pharmacies, supermarkets and discount retailers will continue operating with reduced hours. The annual pause comes just as the US holiday shopping season gathers momentum, with retailers preparing for one of the busiest shopping days of the year.Which major retailers will be closed on Thanksgiving?Walmart, Target, Costco and Best Buy will keep their US stores closed throughout Thanksgiving Day. The companies are expected to resume operations on Black Friday, with several stores opening earlier than their usual business hours.Here is a look at the schedules:Retailer Thanksgiving - November 26 Black Friday, November 27Walmart - Closed - Opens at 6 amTarget - Closed - Opens at 6 amCostco - Closed Executive members at 9 am; other members at 10 amBest Buy - Closed- Opens at 6 amMacy’s - Closed 6 am to 11 pmKohl’s - Closed 5 am to midnightDollar General - 7 am to 8 pm in most states Check local hoursWalgreens Most stores - open 8 am to 5 pm Regular operationsThe timings have been reported by AP and corroborated in holiday shopping coverage by The Independent. Individual store schedules may vary, so customers are advised to check their local outlets before travelling.Grocery stores will follow different holiday schedulesUnlike large department stores and warehouse retailers, several supermarket chains will remain open on Thanksgiving, although many will operate with shorter hours. Kroger, Albertsons, Safeway and Sprouts are among the chains expected to offer limited shopping hours. Whole Foods will also open at selected locations, with some stores closing earlier than usual.However, shoppers looking to visit Aldi, Trader Joe’s or Publix will find their stores closed for the day. Hy-Vee will offer a limited service, allowing customers to collect pre-ordered holiday meals between 8 am and 11 am. These differences make it important for customers to check individual store listings, particularly when planning last-minute grocery purchases.Walgreens and other essential servicesNot every retailer will shut down for Thanksgiving. Walgreens has confirmed that its nearly 8,000 stores will remain open, with most locations operating between 8 am and 5 pm. Pharmacies will be available at approximately half of its locations, while stores that operate around the clock will continue their 24-hour services.Other essential services will see temporary disruptions. Federal government offices, post offices and courts will remain closed on Thursday and reopen on Friday. Banks, including Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, will also shut their physical branches for the holiday. Customers will still be able to access ATMs and mobile banking services.The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq will remain closed on Thanksgiving before resuming trading on Friday. However, Friday’s trading session will be shorter than usual, ending at 1 pm Eastern Standard Time.FedEx and UPS to pause regular deliveriesPeople expecting parcels around Thanksgiving should also account for changes in delivery schedules. FedEx and UPS will suspend their standard pickup and delivery services on Thursday, although certain critical services may remain available at selected locations. Both companies are scheduled to resume normal operations on Friday.With major retailers reopening early and Black Friday promotions beginning, shoppers are expected to return to stores in large numbers on November 27. For customers planning to take advantage of the sales, checking store-specific timings and making purchases ahead of Thanksgiving could help avoid unnecessary trips during the holiday closure.You use AI every day. articles.title: Leonardo DiCaprio joins fight with fewer than 1,000 individuals trying to save a critically endangered Chilean frog from a power project involving 72 towers
articles.summary: Actor and environmental activist Leonardo DiCaprio has joined conservationists in raising concerns over a power transmission project in Chile that could
articles.body: Actor and environmental activist Leonardo DiCaprio has joined conservationists in raising concerns over a power transmission project in Chile that could threaten the survival of a critically endangered frog. Fewer than 1,000 Pehuenche spiny frogs are believed to remain in the wild, with the species confined to a small area of the Andes. The proposed electricity link between Chile and Argentina includes dozens of high-voltage towers planned across the frog’s known habitat. The project got rejected by an environmental commission citing protected natural areas and nature tourism.Leonardo DiCaprio raises alarm over Chilean frog and power projectDiCaprio brought international attention to the issue through an Instagram post in which he shared photographs of the Pehuenche frog and its natural surroundings. According to EL PAÍS, the actor warned that Chile could approve a plan that would destroy the heart of the species' only known habitat.He also tagged the Chilean Herpetological Network, drawing attention to the concerns that conservationists had been raising for years. His intervention came as the project approached an important stage in Chile's environmental approval process.However, DiCaprio clarified that the campaign was not calling for the entire electricity project to be abandoned. Instead, he supported finding an alternative route that would allow the transmission line to be built without putting the frog at greater risk.The Pehuenche frog survives in a restricted mountain habitatThe Pehuenche spiny frog, scientifically known as Alsodes pehuenche, is found in the high Andes along the Chile-Argentina border. Its known habitat includes the Alto Maule region and the Pehuenche Valley in central Chile.According to EL PAÍS, the species lives in small streams and wetlands supplied by melting snow and glaciers. These habitats are located at elevations above 2,000 metres, making the frog particularly dependent on the conditions of its mountain environment.The species was classified as critically endangered in 2018 and has not recovered from that status. Biologist Claudio Azat, director of the One Health Institute and co-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature's amphibian specialist group, told EL PAÍS that its population is estimated at around 1,000 individuals.The frog also has some unusual physical characteristics. During the breeding season, males develop patches of gelatinous spines on their chests and fingers. Their forearms become enlarged, helping them hold onto females during mating. This feature has earned the amphibian the nickname Popeye frog.Its limited distribution makes the species especially vulnerable to changes in its surroundings. Unlike animals that can move to other suitable habitats when their environment is disturbed, the Pehuenche frog has very few places where it can survive.The 72-tower transmission plan has raised environmental concernsThe proposed Los Cóndores-Río Diamante project is being developed by Enel Generación Chile. It is designed to connect the electricity systems of Chile and Argentina through a 500-kilovolt transmission line.According to EL PAÍS, the Chilean section of the project includes a 26.6-kilometre overhead transmission line and 72 high-voltage towers. Conservationists have raised concerns because the planned infrastructure would pass directly through the Pehuenche frog's habitat.The development has been under consideration for nearly 5 years. Its construction would also require supporting infrastructure, including access roads, construction camps and helipads, which could affect the surrounding landscape.El Ciudadano reported that local residents, scientists and environmental campaigners fear these activities could damage the natural environment of Alto Maule. The region is also valued for scientific research, nature tourism and conservation efforts.The proposed route has become a source of concern beyond the survival of one amphibian. Residents and campaigners believe the development could affect the area's wider ecological value and its potential to become a UNESCO-recognised Geopark.Chile's environmental review has stalled the electricity projectDiCaprio's intervention came shortly before a scheduled decision by Chile's Environmental Assessment Commission. The Environmental Assessment Service had recommended approval, but the commission's planned meeting on 10 August 2026 was suspended.The situation subsequently moved beyond a temporary postponement. According to Latin American Post, the Maule Environmental Evaluation Commission rejected the project on 20 August, citing concerns involving biodiversity and tourism.The dispute highlights the challenge of balancing energy needs and conservationThe transmission project was designed to improve electricity connections between Chile and Argentina. The proposed link could help Chile move surplus solar electricity and provide access to electricity generated in Argentina, particularly during periods of changing demand.The two countries have different energy resources and requirements. Chile produces substantial solar power during daylight hours, while Argentina has natural gas reserves and power plants that could help supply electricity at other times. Claudio Azat recalled DiCaprio’s earlier support in 2019 for efforts to protect the Loa frog in Chile.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Dar-e-Nijaat: Pakistani TV drama screenings cancelled in India after backlash
articles.summary: The show, Dar-e-Nijaat, has become a sensation in India but is now embroiled in a political row.
articles.body:
Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.

Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.

The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.

The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.

A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.

In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".

As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.

The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.

Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.

In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.

The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.

The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.

India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.

And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again .

The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.

By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.

Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.

But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.

On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists , in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.

Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.

Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.

For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar , Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.

But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.

Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.

Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.

Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".

It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.

What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.

"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

articles.title: Thanksgiving and National Day of Mourning: What is the history?
articles.summary: Indigenous activists challenge Thanksgiving narratives and highlight ongoing struggles for sovereignty and recognition.
articles.body:
As millions of people across the United States meet with famiy and friends to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, Indigenous people and their supporters will gather in Plymouth, Massachusetts, to mark the 57th annual National Day of Mourning.

For many Indigenous people, the traditional story of Thanksgiving overlooks centuries of colonisation, land dispossession and forced displacement.

But Indigenous activists say the day is also an opportunity to highlight the issues their communities continue to face, from the fight for sovereignty and the protection of their ancestral lands to the struggle to have their voices heard throughout the year.

When are Thanksgiving and the National Day of Mourning in 2026?

In the US, Thanksgiving Day is celebrated every year on the fourth Thursday of November; this year it falls on Thursday, November 26.

In 1863, during the US Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving to be observed on the last Thursday of November.

In 1941, Congress officially established the fourth Thursday of November as Thanksgiving Day.

The National Day of Mourning is observed on the same day. It’s an annual Indigenous-led gathering and protest held to honour Indigenous ancestors, challenge mainstream Thanksgiving narratives and draw attention to the ongoing struggles of Indigenous peoples. It was first held in Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1970.

Other Indigenous-led gatherings and ceremonies take place elsewhere in the US, including the Indigenous Peoples Thanksgiving Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in California.

The US celebration commonly goes back to the autumn of 1621, when English settlers and members of the Wampanoag came together for a three-day harvest celebration in what is now Plymouth, Massachusetts.

But the tradition of giving thanks among Indigenous peoples goes way back before the arrival of European settlers.

“It did not take colonisation to bring a concept of Thanksgiving to this continent,” Jean-Luc Pierite, president of the North American Indian Center of Boston, told Al Jazeera.

“For Indigenous peoples, we have had our ways of feasting, of expressing gratitude, of being in community,” he said.

In November 1620, a group of 102 colonists on board the Mayflower reached present-day Massachusetts. They later established a settlement known as Plymouth on the ancestral lands of the Wampanoag people, at the site of a village known as Patuxet.

Their arrival followed a series of devastating epidemics associated with European contact that had killed many Indigenous people in the region.

In March 1621, the Wampanoag leader Ousamequin, also known as Massasoit, established an alliance with the English settlers for mutual protection.

Later that year, at least 90 Wampanoag men and about 50 English settlers took part in a harvest gathering that would later become known as the “first Thanksgiving”. The moment was documented by English settler Edward Winslow.

This meeting became part of a story of friendship and cooperation between European settlers and Indigenous peoples.

But some Indigenous activists and leaders have contested that narrative, saying it ignores the broader history of colonisation, land dispossession and displacement.

It was more than two centuries after the gathering, in 1863, that Lincoln proclaimed a national day of Thanksgiving.

The proclamation came in the middle of the American Civil War and followed a years-long campaign led by Sarah Josepha Hale, a writer and editor best known as the author of Mary Had a Little Lamb.

What does the traditional Thanksgiving story leave out?

For some, the popular Thanksgiving narrative ignores centuries of violence, land dispossession and forced displacement.

“There is a sanitised version of history in which settlers and Indigenous peoples come together and share a meal,” Pierite said.

He said that this portrayal overlooks the loss of Indigenous lands and lives over the past 400 years.

As European settlements expanded, the Indigenous peoples lost enormous parts of their traditional lands through war, forced relocation and broken treaties.

In 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act, which led to the forced displacement of tens of thousands of Indigenous peoples from their homelands.

Later legislation broadened the reservation system and permitted ownership of tribal lands by non-Indigenous people. Indigenous landholdings declined from about 138 million acres (56 million hectares) in 1887 to 48 million acres (19 million hectares) in 1934.

“More than 400 years after the arrival of the Mayflower, Indigenous people are still denied basic human rights and full control of their own homelands,” Kisha James, co-leader of the United American Indians of New England (UAINE), who is Aquinnah Wampanoag and Oglala Lakota, said in a statement.

What is the National Day of Mourning, and why did it begin?

The National Day of Mourning was first held in 1970 after Wamsutta Frank James , an Aquinnah Wampanoag activist, was invited to speak at an event marking the 350th anniversary of the Pilgrims’ arrival.

After the organisers objected to his speech on the history of violence, land seizure and treatment of Indigenous peoples, James refused to deliver a different version.

Instead, Indigenous people and their supporters gathered in Plymouth on Thanksgiving Day, starting what would become an annual protest .

The gathering, organised by the United American Indians of New England (UAINE), has since become a day of remembrance, resistance and advocacy for Indigenous rights.

Today, James’s granddaughter, Kisha James, is a co-leader of UAINE.

“We are still facing many of the issues that our elders talked about in 1970 at the first National Day of Mourning,” she said in a statement ahead of this year’s gathering.

Pierite said the gathering has grown over the years, attracting both Indigenous and non-Indigenous participants.

“We’re seeing thousands of people gather with us, whether they are Indigenous or not,” he said.

How does the National Day of Mourning relate to other Indigenous struggles around the world?

Pierite said the gathering has also become a platform for expressing solidarity with Indigenous peoples and other communities around the world.

Since October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-led attack on southern Israel was followed by Israel’s war on Gaza, Palestinian speakers have been invited to participate in the National Day of Mourning and speak about their experiences, he said.

He drew parallels between the displacement of Indigenous peoples in the US and Palestinian demands for the right of return, as well as the Indigenous Land Back movement.

“We see these different causes in a very interconnected way,” he said.

“The histories that we have experienced, the suffering that we have experienced, we see that reflected in what is going on in the world today,” Pierite added.

Mahtowin Munro, co-leader of UAINE, said this year’s gathering would also express solidarity with Indigenous communities opposing mining, pipelines, resource extraction and large dams on their lands.

“From Peru to British Columbia, from Boston to the Amazon, Indigenous peoples are defending their sovereignty, calling for land back, and insisting that nothing should happen on their lands without their freely given consent,” Munro said in a statement.

“Indigenous solidarity and resistance are international.”

Why do Indigenous activists call for recognition beyond Thanksgiving?

For some, Thanksgiving also highlights a broader issue: the attention their communities receive around this time of the year and how often their struggles are not recognised during the rest of the year.

“This is a bit of a pain point for our communities because often … we get relegated to the months of October and November,” Pierite said.

He said a lot of the attention is centred around commemorations such as Indigenous Peoples’ Day and the National Day of Mourning. While these occasions help raise public awareness, he said, what’s needed is for people to be more aware of Indigenous issues all year round.

Pierite also highlighted the role of Indigenous peoples in addressing climate change and protecting the environment, saying their voices often struggle to be heard against corporate interests.

“We really need to have these types of platforms and this type of coalition building … so that everybody in the world can build a just and sustainable future,” he said.

James also called for greater recognition of Indigenous perspectives on environmental issues.

“We call on non-Native people to listen to Indigenous voices, especially about how to address the climate crisis,” she said in a statement.

How are Indigenous communities marking the day in 2026?

In Plymouth, Massachusetts, Indigenous people and their supporters are expected to gather at noon (17:00 GMT) near the statue of Massasoit on Cole’s Hill for the 57th annual National Day of Mourning.

According to UAINE, this year’s gathering will highlight issues including missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls and Two-Spirit people, federal funding cuts, Indigenous sovereignty and environmental protection.

On the West Coast, the International Indian Treaty Council (IITC) is holding its annual Indigenous Peoples Thanksgiving Sunrise Gathering on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco, California.

The gathering commemorates the Indigenous occupation of Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971, which helped galvanise the Indigenous rights movement in the US.

Organisers said the gathering honours the resistance of Indigenous ancestors and expresses gratitude for the survival of Indigenous peoples, cultures and ways of life.

Other communities mark this time of year through family gatherings, community meals and expressions of gratitude.

In Washington state, for example, elders of the Muckleshoot Tribe gathered on November 16 for an annual meal celebrating family, friendship and community.

articles.title: A Toronto schoolgirl picked up a stone point at Fort York in 1935 and kept it for 80 years; it was later dated to 4,000-6,000 years ago
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of a Toronto schoolgirl who uncovered a 4,000-6,000-year-old quartzite projectile point during a school trip to Fort York, shedding light on the ancient history of First Nations in the area.
articles.body: According to the Friends of Fort York newsletter, a school trip to Fort York in Toronto in 1935 gave ten-year-old Jeanne Carter an unusual souvenir. While walking along a sandy path towards a building, she noticed a small white stone on the ground and picked it up. She had no idea how old it was or why it might be important. Carter kept the artefact in her curio cabinet for about eighty years until a historian analysed it and found it had been made 4,000 to 6,000 years ago. The artefact was a quartzite projectile point, which dated back to the Archaic period in the Indigenous history of that place. It provided insight into the history of the area many years prior to the establishment of Fort York as a military installation.A small discovery during a school tripThe stone was found by Carter at the Fort York field trip in 1935. In one of her recollections, Carter remembered approaching a building on a sandy track where she saw a white piece. She picked it up and took it back home. It spent nearly eight decades in her curio cabinet before it was given by Carter to her friend working in the museum. This friend then handed it over to Richard Gerrard, a historian in the City of Toronto who identified the archaeological value of the item. According to the Friends of Fort York, the stone was made from quartzite. Gerrard considered the material unusual for this part of Ontario, raising the possibility that it had travelled a considerable distance through trade or movement between communities.A tool in the Archaic periodThis item was estimated to be 4,000 to 6,000 years old; hence, it belonged to the Archaic period, a broad period of Indigenous history prior to the arrival of Europeans. Projectile points were part of Indigenous technologies and as Ontario Parks notes, were often used for hunting or butchering, yet no clear application of Carter's artefact had been defined. Neither the identity of its original owner nor the circumstances behind how it ended up at Fort York had been determined. The fact that it was made of quartzite was especially intriguing. Gerrard proposed that the arrival of this material in Toronto could indicate long-distance migration or trade. No information was provided about the origin of the rock used for creating this artefact.One of only four projectilesWhat made Carter's discovery unique was that it was one of just four projectile points ever found at Fort York, according to the Friends of Fort York newsletter. The other three were uncovered during excavations conducted by archaeologists. Carter, in turn, made her discovery while walking through the site during her field trip. Moreover, the artefact proved to be one of the oldest items in the City of Toronto's collection, according to the Friends of Fort York newsletter, which demonstrated that there was a lot of history hidden under the current urban environment. It was generally known that Fort York was strongly connected with Toronto's military history, namely with the War of 1812.The findings showed that people used the area for thousands of years before the fort was built. According to Wayne Reeves, who is the chief curator of Museums and Heritage Services, the archaeological material demonstrated the presence of First Nations over thousands of years. This kind of item is important historical proof because the Archaic period predates written records in the region, so archaeological finds are essential to knowing the story of the people who lived there. Having been in the possession of Carter for almost 80 years, the point was finally donated and the Friends of Fort York newsletter describes it as one of the oldest artefacts in the City of Toronto's collection.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why has North Korea expelled a Swiss diplomat from Pyongyang?
articles.summary: At the centre of the diplomatic dispute lies the Songdowon International Children’s Camp.
articles.body:
North Korea has expelled the head of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in its capital amid a sanctions row, only weeks after Bern reopened an office and the Swiss foreign minister discussed normalising relations.

According to North Korea’s foreign ministry on Wednesday, the decision to expel the diplomatic representative stemmed from Switzerland’s decision to impose sanctions on the Songdowon International Children’s Camp.

A day earlier, Kim Yo Jong, one of Pyongyang’s top foreign policy officials and sister to leader Kim Jong Un, described the sanctions as an “open hostile act” and an infringement of the North’s sovereignty, in a statement.

She said the camp supported “legitimate” cooperation between North Korea and Russia but didn’t directly address Western accusations that some Ukrainian children abducted by Russian forces were sent there to be “re-educated”.

According to a statement by the foreign ministry carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the head of the Swiss diplomatic office, Sylvain Astier, was summoned and handed a memorandum calling on him to close the office.

“The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours,” the ministry said.

“Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us.”

Responding to the move, the Swiss foreign ministry said relations with Pyongyang would continue through its embassy in the Chinese capital, Beijing, and through North Korea’s embassy in Bern.

It added that it regretted the decision and was arranging for Astier to return to the Beijing embassy.

“The closure of the office does not call into question diplomatic relations between Switzerland and North Korea,” the ministry said.

Late last month, Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis travelled to Pyongyang as Bern opened the office and held talks with senior North Korean officials, including his counterpart, Choe Son Hui, on “promoting dialogue and cooperation”, KCNA said at the time.

At the centre of the diplomatic dispute lies the Songdowon International Children’s Camp, which has been accused of hosting and attempting to indoctrinate children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

On Tuesday, Switzerland added the camp to its sanctions list over its alleged role in the transfer of these children and said it would consider closing its diplomatic office in Pyongyang.

Closely allied with Russia, North Korea has supported Moscow’s war efforts by sending thousands of troops and weapons.

Adding the camp to its list of sanctions, Swiss authorities said the facility exposes children to propaganda and activities designed to promote pro-Russia narratives.

The United Kingdom in May and the European Union in September imposed similar sanctions on the camp, freezing its assets and banning financial transactions with the facility.

What’s the status of North Korean–Swiss relations?

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain diplomatic relations with North Korea and established relations in 1974.

Reportedly, both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong attended school in Switzerland as teenagers in the 1990s.

In 1997, the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation opened a “cooperation office” in the North Korean capital that focused on humanitarian programmes.

In 2020, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the office shut as Pyongyang closed its borders.

articles.title: Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
articles.summary: Russian forces launch ballistic missile attack on Ukrainian capital Kyiv, hitting a shopping centre and other buildings.
articles.body:
At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in a ballistic missile assault.

“Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye,” Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday.

Earlier, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

Russian authorities also reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region and in the city of Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.

Russia has claimed the annexation of the southern region of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022.

The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was targeted with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, with warnings for residents to remain in shelters still in place, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Interfax news agency reported.

The Defence Ministry also said Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa in the Black Sea overnight, according to the news agency. The ministry alleged the ship was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the residents heard loud ballistic missile impact sounds late on Wednesday, which injured at least seven people.

“People who live in certain areas of the city that come under frequent attack, they go and spend their nights in the shelter, even before air raid sirens raise alarm,” she said. “Coming into this winter, Russia has really heightened its attacks, especially on energy facilities.”

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia “is putting pressure on Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining its air defences, and everything that can support military supply chains”.

“Russia has also been hitting power plants ahead of cold weather. The aim is to wear down morale and inflict economic damage, in addition to all these military effects,” she added.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, as a number of the combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region have repeatedly gone offline due to attacks.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued on Wednesday after meeting in Florida.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added.

The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes after the US leader described Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin.

“For us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy told CNN.

articles.title: Kenya gov’t violated constitution with Ebola quarantine site, court says
articles.summary: Kenya’s High Court orders halt to ⁠further works at quarantine facility until details of deal with US are disclosed.
articles.body:
A court in Kenya has ruled that the government breached ⁠the constitution in allowing the ⁠construction of a United States-backed Ebola quarantine facility at a military airbase in the country.

High Court Judge Patricia Nyaundi said on Thursday that the government should have disclosed the details of the agreement with the US and sought public input before signing the deal on the facility near the town of Nanyuki in central Kenya.

The court ordered that any ⁠further works at the quarantine facility be stopped until the government meets these conditions.

“Put differently, the petitioners, the people of Kenya and more significantly, the residents of Laikipia County have been left with the position of persons standing outside the sealed wooden window, straining to discern what is ⁠taking place on the other side,” Nyaundi said in her ruling.

“They are aware ⁠that the decisions affecting their community are being made and implemented, yet they have been denied any meaningful opportunity to know, interrogate or participate in those decisions.”

The 50-bed ⁠facility, located inside Laikipia airbase near Nanyuki, was intended to quarantine people exposed to Ebola, including US citizens. Seven American aid workers who had been ‌in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to help tackle the Ebola outbreak quarantined at the facility in July.

Kenyans have staged angry protests against the facility, as residents accuse the US of offloading Ebola risks onto Kenyans. In June, at least one person was killed after Kenyan police opened fire at demonstrators protesting against the facility.

The week before, hundreds took to the streets in Nanyuki amid growing frustration among residents as Kenyan and US authorities publicly reaffirmed their commitment to the plan despite court orders. At the time, the demonstration also turned violent, with at least two people killed and one wounded.

Kenya’s High Court had temporarily suspended the facility’s construction in late May, but it found ⁠that Health Minister Aden Duale failed to comply with the orders. Duale later told the court he had ordered an immediate halt to construction ⁠and related activity at the site.

Kenya reported its first imported case of the Bundibugyo Ebola ‌strain in early October in a traveller who had arrived from the DRC via Uganda. As of mid-November, Kenya had recorded two deaths and seven other cases, all of whom have recovered. No new cases ‌have been reported in Kenya since October 19.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for the outbreak, which the World Health Organization declared an international public health emergency on May 17.

The government has not yet commented on Thursday’s court ruling.

articles.title: An Alaska pilot who grew up in a village with no roads or shops revived an old Thanksgiving tradition in her single-engine plane, dropping frozen turkeys in burlap sacks to remote families every year since 2022
articles.summary: Experience the heartwarming story of Esther Keim, an Alaska pilot who resurrects an old Thanksgiving tradition by dropping frozen turkeys from her plane to remote families, connecting communities and spreading joy across the winter landscape.
articles.body: For families living in remote parts of Alaska, a Thanksgiving turkey can arrive in an unusual way: falling from the sky in a burlap sack. Pilot Esther Keim has been bringing back this annual surprise since 2022, continuing a tradition started decades ago by a local aviator who once made the holiday special for her hometown.Keim flies her single-engine Stinson over isolated homes and communities, releasing frozen turkeys secured in specially prepared sacks. The deliveries, known as the ‘Alaska Turkey Bomb’, are intended to help families celebrate Thanksgiving while reminding them that they have not been forgotten.The initiative is also a tribute to Kenny Hughes, the pilot whose generosity left a lasting impression on Keim when she was growing up in Skwentna.How a childhood memory inspired the Alaska Turkey BombSkwentna, where Keim spent her childhood, is a small Alaskan community without road connections, grocery stores or a conventional electricity grid. Residents depend on aircraft, riverboats and snow machines to bring in supplies, making food storage and planning particularly important during the long winter months.According to SunnySkyz, Hughes had made a habit of flying over remote homes before Thanksgiving and dropping turkeys for families. His deliveries became a much-anticipated part of the holiday for residents, including Keim, who remembers the small gestures he made for children.She recalled how Hughes would sometimes drop a newspaper containing a pack of gum. For children who could not simply walk into a shop to buy something, even that modest gift carried considerable meaning.Years later, Keim found herself in a position to bring the tradition back. By then, she had moved to Wasilla, become a private pilot and purchased her first aircraft.The idea took shape during a visit to Skwentna in spring 2022. While speaking to a local family, she heard about the difficulties they had faced getting through the winter. The father described their limited food supply with a remark that stayed with her."One squirrel doesn't split three ways very far for dinner," he told her.The conversation brought back memories of Hughes and his Thanksgiving flights. Keim realised she could use her own aircraft to offer similar help to families in the area. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Esther Sanderlin-Keim (@akbrunette)]]>From three dozen turkeys to an annual Thanksgiving traditionKeim's first delivery run took place that Thanksgiving in 2022. She distributed 36 frozen turkeys across an area covering approximately 75 miles of remote Alaska, as per the outlet.People began contributing to the initiative as news of the effort spread. Volunteers also stitched burlap sacks to carry the frozen birds, securing them with bright yellow tape to make the packages easier to identify against the snow.What began as a tribute to Hughes has since become an annual effort. articles.body: After more than a year apart, Marine Cpl. Dominic Morimando surprised his mother with a visit home for the holidays through a program that allows service members to earn flights home by volunteering. He told "Fox & Friends Weekend" on Sunday that the enthusiasm of the students he worked with made the experience rewarding. "It was such a great experience because they are so excited and so happy to have us there, and I was able to accumulate so many hours," the corporal said. articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García leaves for Spain. But the Trump administration got what it wanted
articles.summary: His departure ends a high-profile legal battle over due process and deportation, but leaves the Trump administration facing little accountability for its act...
articles.body:
Kilmar Ábrego García , the man illegally deported to his native El Salvador last year and whose immigration case spurred a 20-month-long battle with the Trump administration, arrived in Spain on Wednesday.

Trump administration officials and Ábrego García supporters are both claiming voluntary departure from the US to avoid deportation is a victory for their respective sides.

And they're both sort of right, if such an ugly immigration spectacle can even be associated with concepts of victory.

On the one hand, Ábrego García has the relief of leaving the country seemingly his own accord, given that he was not going to be allowed to remain legally in the US. By going to Spain he avoids the pitfalls he had been facing. These were: being indefinitely detained inside a horrific prison in El Salvador, being sent to an unfamiliar African country where, if some other examples are anything to go by, he could end up in a prison or detained under harsh conditions in a secured hotel, indefinitely, or detained indefinitely in a US cell. His attorneys hope that, under a different president in the future, he may be allowed to return to the US.

And on the other hand, the Trump administration has won by getting rid of a high-profile immigrant they were determined not to let rest.

Ábrego García first arrived in the spotlight in March 2025, after the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador despite a US court order protecting him from being deported there , for his own safety. His case led to a nearly two-year-long "David and Goliath" type battle between him and the Trump administration, raising concerns about due process and constitutional rights, the separation of powers and accountability, the US government's deals with countries for deportations and questionable federal prosecutions.

The entire case transcends the complicated character of Ábrego García himself. It has shown the world the lengths the Trump administration will go to when carrying out its anti-immigrant crackdown, and was an early example of the emboldened returning president defying federal court orders, to say nothing of fairness.

Ábrego García arrived in the US in 2011 from El Salvador without proper authorization and lived in Maryland for years, regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ). He married a US citizen and had a child with her.

In 2019, he was arrested outside a hardware store in Maryland after local police, relying on an informant and what his lawyers called " no evidence ", accused him of being a gang member. He was turned over to ICE, but a judge ruled he should not be deported to his country of origin due to danger in that country. He continued with his life with a valid work permit.

Then in March 2025, ICE officials arrested him while driving home with his five-year-old son. And after the Trump administration had struck a deal with the Salvadorian government, run by the rightwing and self-proclaimed "world's coolest dictator", Nayib Bukele, ICE quickly deported Ábrego García to El Salvador along with dozens of Venezuelan men in one of the most infamous immigration actions of the second Trump administration. As the flights were midair, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to turn them back , due to accusations of due process violations. The administration defied the federal judge. The men arrived in El Salvador and were violently taken to a notorious anti-terrorism prison called Cecot, ostensibly to be detained indefinitely. Many claimed they were tortured, assaulted, raped and traumatized by the ordeal.

In court filings, the Trump administration admitted they had mistakenly deported Ábrego García due to an "administrative error". After a lengthy legal battle, including input from the US supreme court , the administration was ordered to return him to the US. They initially refused , but eventually he was brought back in June 2025.

The Trump administration then quickly charged him with crimes relating to human smuggling, based on a traffic stop in Tennessee dating from 2022, and he was detained again . In parallel with the criminal case, this allowed ICE to begin attempts to remove him to a series of African countries . Ábrego García and his legal team resisted. Then, presumably concluding he had no future as a free man in the US, he offered to be removed to Costa Rica. The administration refused to send him to the Central American country and pushed to deport him to Africa.

The government denigrated him publicly as a "gang member", "human trafficker", "wife beater" and "child predator". They pointed to accusations that he had allegedly abused his wife. He had never committed any of those crimes.

However, his human smuggling case was dismissed in May of this year, with the federal judge saying it was a "vindictive prosecution".

Negotiations continued behind closed doors. A court order unsealed on Wednesday shows that the federal judge presiding over his case had ordered the Trump administration to effectuate Ábrego García's voluntary departure from the US. The judge ordered the administration not to intervene in his departure. On Tuesday, it was announced he was leaving the US voluntarily, but to Europe, not Central America. He duly arrived in Spain's capital, Madrid, on Wednesday morning with his wife. Competing claims of victory broke out from Ábrego García's supporters and the Trump administration.

"I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this administration's constant persecution," said Senator Chris Van Hollen, who visited Ábrego García in El Salvador and pushed for his return.

"We are delighted to announce that Kilmar Ábrego García has self-deported from the United States to Spain," said homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, using a favored Trump administration phrase when people leave the country specifically to avoid deportation.

The years-long and tired narrative of the "good" immigrant versus "bad" immigrant has only helped immigration hardliners justify the propping up of an aggressive enforcement system that targets all and tramples on due process rights, regardless of criminal history.

One of Ábrego García's attorneys said he is leaving the US because he thought he was "never going to get a fair shake" under the Trump administration. They aren't wrong. But this is purely by design. And his is one case of thousands in which people are not getting a fair shake under an immigration system that resembles more closely punishment than merely civil immigration proceedings.

Ábrego García "humiliated" the Trump administration "because he exposed their failures and beat them in court; even all the way to the Supreme Court", immigration policy analyst Aaron Reichlin-Melnick said on social media . "For that, they tried everything to punish him. And they lost, again and again. Now, they lose a final time: he leaves as a free man."

But the Trump administration does have reason to feel smug. No one in the administration has been held responsible, in any significant way, for the catastrophic Cecot ordeal, its violation of court orders and the alleged torture they helped facilitate. And no one is being held responsible for wielding an immigration enforcement system targeting thousands – although the midterms "blue wave" for the Democrats was certainly a signal of increasing voter opposition.

Ábrego García's departure to Spain means perhaps no more than the closing of a very disturbing chapter in an ongoing horror story.

articles.title: Are Trump’s tariffs aimed at securing US-friendly trade deals?
articles.summary: New US policy threatens further tariff hikes on China, India, Vietnam if trade negotiations fall through.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has proposed a new slate of trade tariffs against 14 of the US’s key trading partners, including China, India and the European Union.

The tariffs, which would go into effect next year, will hit China the hardest, potentially subjecting its products to a 40 percent import tax.

Washington says the tariffs, announced by the US Trade Representative (USTR) on Wednesday, are a response to unfair trading practices which harm US manufacturing, including “excess industrial capacity” – subsidies and policies that enable manufacturers to overproduce and undercut the US.

But Trump has long used tariffs as leverage in trade negotiations.

So, is the latest tariff announcement an effort to win concessions in upcoming trade deals? Here’s what we know:

Which economies do the tariffs target, and when would they start?

The tariffs would be imposed on products from China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to the USTR. The maximum rates facing each country range from 20 percent to 40 percent.

It is unclear when exactly the tariffs would take effect, but a senior US official told the AFP news agency they would likely start in January at the earliest.

Trump has launched several rounds of trade tariffs against other countries and economies during his second term in office, with his administration citing various laws and justifications for the policies each time.

In April 2025, Trump imposed a sweeping raft of import taxes against almost all US trade partners, known as the “Liberation Day” tariffs. He said the measures were retaliation for unfair trade practices, including high tariffs, against the US that hurt local manufacturing. Trump imposed those tariffs under an emergency powers law, but the Supreme Court struck them down in February this year.

Then, in July, Washington cited a different law – section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 – to impose more tariffs on more than 80 countries. This time, Trump’s administration claimed the targeted countries had failed to adequately restrict imported goods made with forced labour.

The latest tariff announcement also cites section 301 of the same trade act, which allows Washington to penalise countries it determines are treating US businesses unfairly. It follows an eight-month investigation into what Washington calls “structural excess capacity”, by which governments give their industries unfair advantages with subsidies, suppressed wages and other policies.

Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners were using “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base”.

Inga Fechner, a senior economist at ING THINK, wrote that “while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind.”

Is this really about clinching better trade deals for the US?

For several targeted countries, that appears to be a big factor.

The tariff announcement comes as the US negotiates trade agreements with several of the targeted countries, including China, India, Vietnam and Singapore, with some of the proposed tariff rates explicitly linked to the outcome of those talks.

China’s tariffs are due to rise by 20 percent, respecting a cap under a current US-China trade truce. But if talks to secure a new trade deal fail by January 10, when that truce is due to expire, the rate could double to up to 40 percent, according to USTR.

Vietnam would also be subject to a capped tariff rate of 20 percent if it makes a trade deal with Washington, which it is actively negotiating. But if those negotiations fall through, its rate would jump to 35 percent.

India would face a 17 percent tariff rate if a trade agreement is reached with Washington, but a 25 percent rate if not.

Singapore faces a 10 percent tariff if it reaches a trade deal with the US, but a 20 percent rate if not.

Madeline Chalecki, assistant director at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, said the US is also exercising leverage over Mexico, which Trump recently said the US is close to concluding a trade deal with. Mexico was among the countries included in the USTR’s excess capacity investigation, but has not yet been hit with new tariffs.

“The threat of additional tariffs may be a better negotiating chip than the duties themselves,” the Atlantic Council quoted Chalecki as saying.

Mona Paulsen, an assistant professor at the London School of Economics and Political Science Law School, told Al Jazeera that beyond tariffs, the bigger worry regarding US trade negotiations is whether they are “from the beginning, an asymmetrical exercise more calibrated to US economic growth, and less one about two (or more) partners cooperating”.

Some of the targeted countries or blocs have criticised the US’s new tariffs , while others have pledged to step up efforts to pursue trade deals with the US.

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun accused the US of engaging in “political manipulation”, saying the “so-called ‘overcapacity’ is a false issue”. Commerce Ministry spokesman He Yadong called on the US to “correct its erroneous practices” and said Beijing reserves the right to “take necessary measures” in response.

Singapore also called on the US to reevaluate ⁠the policy, which it expressed disappointment over.

India said any trade concerns between it and the US should be resolved in ongoing trade negotiations.

Vietnam said it was working to conclude a trade pact with the US and promised to address the “overcapacity” issue and to improve forced labour regulations.

The EU’s trade commissioner, ⁠Maros Sefcovic, ⁠said he strongly opposed the US tariff move, adding that Washington must abide by the 15 percent tariff limit it has already agreed for goods imported from the bloc.

Why else might Trump be imposing new tariffs now?

Several analysts say Trump is trying to set up a long-term tariff infrastructure, despite the Supreme Court striking down his “Liberation Day” tariffs earlier this year.

Josh Lipsky, vice president and chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council, said the Trump administration’s latest announcement appears to be an attempt to set up a “tariff web – one meant to stick past this administration”.

Gregory Shaffer, professor of international law at the Georgetown University Law Center, told Al Jazeera that Trump is trying to “set tariffs globally” without having to deal with Congress.

US Senator Ron Wyden, a Democrat who is expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee in next year’s Congress, called the tariff move “a blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs”.

“Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” said Wyden.

articles.title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
articles.summary: The changes could see drivers over 70 stripped of licences if they do not meet standards.
articles.body:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail .

Drivers over 70 to face eye tests every three years

The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive.

The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous.

A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue.

"One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years.

The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over.

A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents.

"Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this.

"We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about."

articles.title: Iraq denies reports of troop movements towards Kurdish region
articles.summary: Government says there is ‘no truth’ to media reports that Iraqi army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region.
articles.body:
Iraq’s government has denied local media reports that army units were moving towards the Kurdistan region, as a top court backed Baghdad’s authority over the region’s border crossings and oil in a deepening dispute with Erbil.

Government spokesperson Haidar al-Aboudi told state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya on Wednesday that there was “no truth” to the media reports. He said oil smugglers were diverting “tens of billions” into “private pockets and accounts”, and that the salaries of Kurdistan’s public employees were not part of the dispute.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said “national sovereignty is indivisible” and that protecting Iraq’s wealth was “a battle for existence” in which the state would end all forms of smuggling.

Al-Zaidi has ordered the Border Ports Authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdistan region and to close unofficial crossings. He has also ordered federal authorities to take over oil fields in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahuddin and Diyala that are under Kurdish security control.

Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court has issued an interpretive ruling affirming federal powers to secure international borders and deploy armed forces across all Iraqi territory. It also affirmed Baghdad’s right to oversee border crossings, including those in Kurdistan, the production and export of oil and gas, and both oil and non-oil revenues.

Border Forces Commander Mohammed Abdul Wahab Sukkar al-Saidi told the state-run Iraqi News Agency on Thursday that the command had “begun implementing the directive of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces to close all unofficial crossings” with neighbouring countries.

He did not say how many crossings would be affected.

The Kurdistan Regional Government’s council of ministers, chaired by Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, said it rejected “any attempt to return Iraq to a centralised system”. Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani rejected addressing the region in “military language”, saying this “does not solve any problem”.

Thousands of people gathered in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdish region, on Thursday to protest against the government’s plan to take over border crossings and oil operations.

Reporting from Erbil, Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdel Wahed said the protesters claim the government’s plan “touches on their sovereignty and their territorial integrity, and that this undermines the constitutional rights of the Kurdish people”.

“The question now is whether or not the government of Baghdad will be able to solve this peacefully without triggering a new chapter of conflict, a new political and economic confrontation with the Kurdish region.”

Baghdad says some 200,000 to 230,000 barrels of oil a day are being smuggled, worth about $200m a month, Al Jazeera correspondent Suhaib al-Asa said.

Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera that the ruling, issued within 24 hours at al-Zaidi’s request, gave Baghdad a legal basis to act. “The court’s decision is final and decisive,” he said. “But the issue is not only constitutional and legal. There is a political problem.”

The country’s four presidencies have agreed to hold a national dialogue on December 1 to resolve the crisis.

The orders followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company, after which al-Zaidi dismissed eight officials, including Kirkuk’s police chief and operations commander.

articles.title: In Manipur, a glass of drinking water comes at a price: Women trek through forests, villagers risk ambushes to repair pipelines amid conflict and drought
articles.summary: IMPHAL: In parts of Manipur, getting drinking water means walking through forests in search of a spring.
articles.body: IMPHAL: In parts of Manipur, getting drinking water means walking through forests in search of a spring. Repairing a broken pipeline can be even more dangerous. In May, villagers from Konsakhul in Kangpokpi were ambushed while attempting to restore a damaged community pipeline. Two months earlier, two youths had died after setting out to repair water pipelines near the Ukhrul-Kamjong border, over 100km away.With Manipur recording a 45% deficit in monsoon rainfall, according to IMD, the onset of winter has brought fresh anxieties for communities already grappling with damaged infrastructure, shrinking natural sources and restrictions on movement.In hilly districts, where direct tap water often remains largely absent outside some district headquarters, villages have traditionally depended on natural springs and rainwater harvesting, according to wetlands and Loktak Lake activist Ram Wangkheirakpam. But several springs are now drying up, leaving communities with fewer reliable sources. “The conflict has made it harder to reach water sources and maintain supply lines,” Wangkheirakpam told TOI.The burden often falls on women, who walk long distances through forested stretches to fetch water. What was once a familiar part of village life has become more difficult as natural sources recede and movement across conflict-divided areas remains fraught.“In districts like Senapati, Ukhrul, and Chandel, villages marked 'covered' on paper, women and children still walk kilometre-long distances daily to fetch water from streams, springs, or community wells,” Wangkheirakpam told TOI, adding that in Imphal, too, municipal taps offer little assurance. “Households receive piped water for barely one to two hours, twice a week... Many have turned to private tankers, paying Rs 300-500 for 500-1,000 litres.”And for the 60,000-plus people displaced by the conflict and living across relief camps, the struggle is more immediate. At Churachandpur’s Tuibung Community Hall, 150 residents from 23 families share three toilets and pool their ?84 daily relief allowance to buy drinking water. At nearby Mandap camp, where 250 people remain in makeshift shelters, only two of eight toilets work—leaving residents like Hatnu, in her twenties, with little privacy to bathe or manage periods alongside a daily struggle for clean water.In Senapati, social activist R K Paul Chawang told TOI villagers “wake up as early as 3.30-4am in the winter cold to collect water from common points”, taking turns with buckets. Along with five Naga communities in 2025, Chawang filed a PIL in Manipur HC over alleged irregularities in Jal Jeevan Mission projects.Contacted for comment, a senior official in the Public Health Engineering Department (PHED), which executes drinking-water projects, said rural coverage was split into two streams: 38% under the Centre's Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM)—still awaiting Gram Sabha certification—and 62% under a New Development Bank-funded project. Work on the latter was progressing, the official said, adding that “discrepancies in online records were being corrected” and “village water supply had improved.”Stay updated with the latest Imphal news. articles.title: This Thanksgiving, ask yourself: What are you taking for granted?
articles.summary: This Thanksgiving, let's focus on gratitude for our health, employment, spouse, parents and friends we too often take for granted.
articles.body: As a young man, I started a church. I poured my life into it. I worked long hours, made big sacrifices and enjoyed every minute of it. Souls were saved, lives were changed, relationships were restored. We made a huge impact. It was the original contemporary-style church in central Virginia. Now there are probably more than 100 such churches. It’s one of the greatest things I’ve ever done with my life. I’m so proud of all that was accomplished. If I had to do it over, I’d do it again. In a heartbeat. THAD ROTHROCK: BIBLE REMINDS US TO KEEP SERVING GOD EVEN AFTER WE RETIRE But after 27 years, I left the church I founded. I did it because I felt God had more for me to do. There were many more people I could inspire. He had a larger plan for my life. I couldn’t give my full focus to the church while writing books, traveling to speak and pursuing media opportunities. It was the right decision. I’m glad I did it. Building facilities, expanding campuses and creating new ministries was exciting. Getting to know thousands of great folks, helping people in need and working with some fantastic, talented staff and volunteers was a joy. But it was exhausting. And with growth comes greater expectations and more entitlement. There is so much we take for granted until it’s gone. Before you know it, people just assume there will always be powerful services, inspiring preaching, engaging children’s ministry — and that is just on Sunday. During the week, they want groups, classes and events. It isn’t great being taken for granted. I think people thought since I started the church I would just stay for 40 years and would always be there whenever needed. It is not the reason I left. It’s the reality I experienced. You don’t serve people for recognition, but you don’t like to feel as if it’s all expected. Thanksgiving is the one day a year we focus on gratitude for the multitude of blessings in our lives. It’s certainly good to be grateful, to take time around the Thanksgiving table and share what we are truly thankful for. But taking time each day to recall all the blessings in your life will help to keep you from taking things for granted. DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT There is much we take for granted until it’s gone. Health is an obvious one. A woman in my church just sent her only child to college. She and her husband now looked forward to a new season in their lives. But instead, she was diagnosed with cancer and within months died. It’s so easy to take your health for granted until you don’t have it. Your job is another example. Two men from my church lost their jobs and have been searching for months for employment. Highly capable and successful, they are still without employment. Having a steady income is necessary to live, and yet it’s not guaranteed. We may not love our job, but it’s better than being without one. TIM MCGRAW WARNS OF ‘MOST DANGEROUS’ TIMES IN MARRIAGE AFTER 30 YEARS WITH FAITH HILL And what about the people we take for granted? We could begin with our spouse. I have been traveling for years, but my wife travels less.
