articles.title: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
articles.summary: Recently bailed activist denies accusations of supporting Hamas, claiming he is being punished for supporting Palestine.
articles.body:
Madrid, Spain – James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government, said he believed the US is targeting supporters of the people of Gaza worldwide.

The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas.

He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.

Chambers, a self-proclaimed Marxist-Leninist and the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune, believes supporters of the Palestinian cause are being targeted around the globe.

“I think that when the neocolonial system starts to break apart economically, militarily, which I believe is happening, it becomes desperate. And when it becomes desperate, it becomes more violent and more violent,” he told Al Jazeera.

“And all these things sort of converge around the occupation of Palestine because we understand the occupation of Palestine as basically nothing more than an expression of US military and business interest. So that is the focal point of repression.”

He added: “In relation to the Palestinian cause and other causes, I think there is a kind of effort certainly in the US to designate [expressing] antiwar ideas as extremist and terrorist.”

‘They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas’

Chambers, who was released from prison in Madrid on bail last week after serving four months on remand, said he was being targeted by the US because of his support for the Palestinian cause.

“I’m not even accused of sending money anywhere illegal. I’m accused of wanting to, which is sort of a crazy distinction to me. They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas, no. They’ve accused me of wanting to send money to Hamas,” he said.

A keen football fan, he said he transferred the money to Club Africain, a Tunisian football team, which he sponsors.

He said he had met someone from the Iranian embassy in Tunisia at an international book fair in 2023.

“[They] tied in a narrative which says that … I allegedly visited the Iranian diplomats, which is not true. I met someone from the Iranian embassy at an international book fair, who told me that US citizens are allowed to have tourist visas. I never met an official at the embassy. I never went into the offices at the embassy.”

The 41-year-old said a forensic accountant had presented Club Africain’s accounts to the Madrid court.

As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023.

“I’m assuming the implication is that I would have met with these people and then transferred money to Tunisia to a football club with the intention of then laundering it to Hamas.”

The US Department of Justice said it did not want to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.

Chambers said he was “very publicly” affiliated with the club, which won the Tunisian championship this year, and he made a four-year sponsorship deal.

“They had millions of euros worth of debt, which is why they contacted me to get involved. And the money was used to pay off debts, to revamp the team facilities, training facilities, youth programmes, pay overdue salaries. And then in return I had some involvement in management,” he said.

Chambers also said Tunisia was a “closed economy”.

“When you move money into Tunisia, you’re not allowed to move it out,” he said, adding that one of his “most constant emotions in all of this is just downright confusion”.

Chambers, who has given financial aid to 100 projects in 20 countries, including some in Palestine, said he was always careful to obey the law.

“There is no smoking gun. There’s no unloaded gun. There’s nowhere that I said I wanted to support any illegal groups,” he said.

Chambers said he was a target for supporting the Palestinian cause.

“I think the combination of an overall effort by the US authorities to criminalise basically the Palestinian cause in any capacity … this is a part of that,” he said. “You know the fact that I happen to have a lot of resources. And I speak out unapologetically and freely about my positions on US imperialism. These things just combined to make me a target and an example.”

Prison staff ‘saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there’

The father-of-four, who has been reunited with his family after being released on bail, is awaiting the court’s decision. His case has also drawn attention to concerns about the implications of the US extradition request.

During his time in jail, he said he received letters of support from many strangers as well as political parties from all sides.

“Even within the prison staff, there was a kind of consensus that people saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there,” he said.

However, he said he faces an uncertain future.

“I still don’t know … whether I am going to face decades of my life in a federal penitentiary in the US,” he said.

The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request. The proceedings have been the subject of further reporting on the extradition case in Spain.

Chambers was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.

He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.

articles.title: 7 iconic Thanksgiving dishes Americans love to hate but keep serving every year
articles.summary: Every Thanksgiving table has a divisive dish, a chef says. From canned cranberry sauce to green bean casserole, here are seven that families keep serving.
articles.body: Every Thanksgiving table has a dish that seems to divide the room. From casseroles to questionable "salads," some holiday fixtures inspire heated reactions — but still end up on the table year after year. "Thanksgiving dishes can bring out strong opinions because they're tied to what people grew up eating," Dennis Littley, a New Jersey-based chef and founder of Ask Chef Dennis, told Fox News Digital. FROM FONDUE TO CASSEROLES: CLASSIC 1960S FOODS THAT DEFINED A GENERATION Some guests love them, Littley said, while others would rather pass. "Families keep serving these dishes because they’re part of the holiday for them," he said. "A beloved family recipe doesn't have to be everyone's favorite to earn a place on the table." Below are seven Thanksgiving dishes that everyone loves to hate — and why families keep serving them anyway. 1. Canned jellied cranberry sauce Cranberry grower Marcus L. Urann began commercially canning cranberry sauce in Massachusetts in 1912, and Ocean Spray, founded in 1930, later helped make it a Thanksgiving staple, according to the company's website. DOLLY PARTON'S FAVORITE SOUTHERN DISHES, FROM CHICKEN AND DUMPLINGS TO BANANA PUDDING While no table is complete without it, fresh and whole-berry alternatives have since entered the space, and the canned version has some harsh critics. In a Reddit thread asking for people's opinions on the "absolutely worst and disgusting side dishes," one person cited "that cranberry gel stuff." The sweetness and texture of dishes like cranberry sauce can be "especially polarizing," Littley said. 2. Green bean casserole Campbell's recipe developer Dorcas Reilly created green bean casserole in 1955 as an easy dish made with staples like green beans and condensed cream of mushroom soup, and it gradually became a Thanksgiving fixture, Littley said. CAMPBELL'S ROLLS OUT NEW SOUPS, INCLUDING FIRST-EVER GLUTEN-FREE CHICKEN NOODLE VARIETY People online are divided over the dish. One Reddit user summed it up as "slimy canned green beans, canned 'onions' and over-salty canned soup." While some roast the dish, others defend it. "I love green bean casserole, but the slander every holiday season cracks me up," one person said. "I can see why it would gross people out, though." 3. Jell-O salads Jell-O salads have seen a revival in the food world recently, with home cooks sharing retro molds online and chefs bringing savory aspics — meat, seafood, eggs or vegetables suspended in a gelatinous broth or consommé — back to restaurant menus, as Fox News Digital previously reported. CLASSIC AMERICAN PANTRY STAPLES ARE GETTING A MAJOR PROTEIN- AND FIBER-PACKED MAKEOVER Jell-O salads still find a place at some family gatherings, too, with some Reddit users describing versions with iceberg lettuce and pimento-stuffed olives, as well as cottage cheese, cheddar, walnuts and raisins. One commenter's mother defends her lime Jell-O salad as "refreshing," while another described their family's marshmallow-and-grape version as "terrifying." 4. Ambrosia salad At many Thanksgiving tables is ambrosia salad, Jell-O salad's even sweeter fruit-filled cousin, usually made with canned pineapple, mandarin oranges, marshmallows and whipped topping. "Someone keeps making ambrosia for some reason," one Redditor said of their family's holiday table. "No one touches it but it’s always there." 7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN’T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON Ambrosia salad was once considered a symbol of luxury on Thanksgiving tables in the 1800s and early 1900s, according to Chowhound. Though it has since fallen out of fashion, it remains a nostalgic Southern favorite and still has some fans. "I love it! But the rest of my family won’t even go near it," one internet user said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES This year, ambrosia salad is also seeing a nostalgic revival as home cooks revisit vintage potluck dishes, sometimes updating it with fresh fruit, real whipped cream or Greek yogurt. 5. Turnips Once considered a "poor man's" vegetable, turnips have a reputation of being bitter if overcooked. One Reddit user said their mom mashes turnips with rutabagas every year. "It's just gross and funky, and she spends so much time every year trying to convince everyone else to 'just try it!'" Finally, last year, the family convinced her not to make it, the person said. "I can't tell you how much I'm looking forward to not being pressured into putting it on my plate this year." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER But not everyone has written the turnip off. "My aunt made a mashed turnip dish that we expected to be gross because it looked gross," one Redditor recalled. "But it surprisingly wasn’t." 6. Coleslaw For Littley, the divisive dish at his family's Thanksgiving table serves a dual purpose. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Our Thanksgiving meal has a tradition that may surprise people: We serve coleslaw," he said. "It may be regional, but we love it with the turkey dinner." "It’s especially good on leftover turkey sandwiches with stuffing and cranberry sauce," he noted. 7. Marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes This dish began as a marketing idea in 1917. The Angelus Marshmallow Company hired recipe developer Janet McKenzie Hill to create dishes featuring marshmallows, according to Smithsonian Magazine. For some diners, the sweet-on-sweet combination is what makes the candy-coated casserole hard to stomach. "My yuck is the classic sweet potato with marshmallows casserole," one Redditor said. "I love sweet potatoes and yams.... I like toasted marshmallows. Together they are yucky." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the commenter summed up the Thanksgiving table standoff: "One person's yum is another person's yuck."

articles.title: New boss appointed to lead Travelodge after boss quit in August
articles.summary: The new CEO will lead the Thame-based company from 1 December following Jo Boydell's resignation.
articles.body:
Travelodge has appointed a former Tui executive to become its new boss from the start of December.

The former CEO of the Oxfordshire-based budget hotel chain Jo Boydell quit in the summer after safety issues were raised at many of its sites.

A woman staying at its Maidenhead hotel was sexually assaulted in December 2022 after a man lied to staff to get a key card to her room. Kyran Smith was jailed for seven-and-a-half years for the attack .

Peter Krueger will start his new role at Travelodge on Tuesday, replacing interim chief Ray Reidy who has led the company since Boydell quit.

She left the company after facing significant criticism over the handling of the sexual assault incident and wider safety concerns.

It prompted former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to urge her to "seriously engage" with the government on the issue after she cancelled a meeting with MPs.

An independent review by Paul Greaney KC published in October found the sexual assault victim was treated in a "disgraceful" way and "fundamentally failed" by the hotel chain.

In an update on Thursday, Reidy said the business is "continuing to make further investments into room security, and the safety and security of our guests remains our top priority".

articles.title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
articles.summary: Officials say the man confessed to travelling at speed and clipping the fuel truck as he was overtaking traffic.
articles.body:
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.

The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.

Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.

Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.

The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".

"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."

At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.

Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.

The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.

A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

articles.title: A Canadian couple added their son to the title of their family farm in 2008, but a falling-out 15 years later led to a legal battle; an appeals court has now recognised his one-third share and ordered a sale
articles.summary: A Canadian couple who added their son's name to the title of their family farm in 2008 have lost their legal battle to prevent its sale after a serious
articles.body: A Canadian couple who added their son's name to the title of their family farm in 2008 have lost their legal battle to prevent its sale after a serious breakdown in their relationship. The Manitoba Court of Appeal has ruled that the son received an immediate one-third ownership interest in the property and directed that the farm be sold.The dispute centred on whether Arthur and Mary Ann Berry had given their son, Paul Sean Berry, an ownership stake in the farm when they added him to the title, or whether he was only meant to inherit an interest after both parents died.In a unanimous ruling delivered on November 12, 2026, the Manitoba Court of Appeal allowed Paul's appeal, overturned the lower court's refusal to order a sale and sent the matter back to the Court of King's Bench to carry out the sale.According to the court's official judgement document, the parents had bought the farm in 1984, when they moved to Canada from the United Kingdom with their three children. Their son was 14 at the time. The property, near Fisher Branch in Manitoba, consists of three adjoining quarter sections of farmland, each registered under a separate title.A gift made in 2008 became the centre of the disputeOn October 27, 2008, Arthur and Mary Ann signed a deed of gift prepared by their lawyer. It stated that they were giving the property to Paul and that the gift was made out of “natural love and affection”. The land title was transferred to the parents and their son as joint tenants on November 13 that year.The parents later maintained that the arrangement came with an understanding: Paul would continue helping with the farm, while they would keep operating it until they were no longer able and would be allowed to live in their farmhouse for the rest of their lives. They said this understanding had not been written into a separate agreement.The family continued farming together, but their accounts of how the arrangement worked differed. According to the parents' evidence before the lower court, Paul left the farm a few months after the transfer to take a full-time job in Arborg. He returned to work on the farm in 2012 and received a monthly wage of 1,200 Canadian dollars.The parents said they continued paying him even though they felt he was not doing the physical work expected of him. Paul, however, gave a different account of his role, saying he had taken over the farm's operations by 2011. These were competing claims recorded in the lower court judgment.Relationship broke down after plans to add daughters to titleAccording to the official judgement document, The family relationship deteriorated in 2023. The parents said the conflict began after they told Paul they wanted their two daughters, Jeanette and Lynette, added to the farm title so that all three children would eventually have an equal interest.Paul's account was different. He alleged that his parents had told him they would not honour their earlier understanding and intended to leave the property to his sisters instead. He also accused his father of threatening him and his wife and damaging farm machinery. The parents denied the allegations and made their own claims about Paul's conduct.The dispute reached the courts. The parents served Paul with a notice of their intention to sever the joint tenancy in October 2024. The title was subsequently changed so that each parent and Paul held an undivided one-third interest as tenants in common. Paul then sought an order for the sale of the farm.Lower court refused to order a saleIn March 2025, the Manitoba Court of King's Bench dismissed Paul's application. The judge concluded that the parents had intended to give their son only a right of survivorship, meaning he would receive the property after their deaths, rather than an ownership interest he could exercise during their lifetimes. Paul appealed the decision.Appeal court says deed showed an immediate giftThe Court of Appeal disagreed with the lower court's interpretation of the 2008 transfer. It said the deed of gift clearly showed that the parents intended to give Paul an immediate interest in the property.The judges noted that the parents' wish to continue living on and farming the land did not contradict shared ownership. As joint tenants, all three had rights in the property.The court also held that the later severance of the joint tenancy left each of the three family members with an undivided one-third interest as tenants in common. Paul therefore had a current ownership interest and the right to apply for a sale.The appeal court also rejected the lower court's use of the clean-hands principle to deny his request. It said the allegations about the farm business and equipment were part of a separate, unresolved dispute and were not directly connected to how Paul had acquired his ownership share in 2008.The Court of Appeal allowed Paul's appeal and directed the sale of the property under Manitoba's Law of Property Act. It sent the matter back to the Court of King's Bench to conduct the sale in accordance with the legislation and court rules. The parents' cross-appeal seeking to have Paul's name removed from the title was dismissed as moot. Paul was also awarded the costs of the appeal and his original application.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Spare 15 minutes to understand its spirit’: Amit Shah takes swipe at Rahul Gandhi on Constitution Day
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday took a swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Constitution Day, urging those who go around holding
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Thursday took a swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Constitution Day, urging those who go around holding copies of the Constitution to spend 15 minutes examining its original illustrations to understand its spirit.Addressing the 'Samvidhan Gaurav Diwas' programme in Delhi, Shah asked Rahul and others to visit the Parliament library and look at the illustrations by artist Nandalal Bose in the original copy of the Constitution."I request those who go around holding the Constitution to visit Parliament's library and spare 15 minutes to understand its spirit through the illustrations by Nandalal Bose," Shah said.He also accused Rahul of seeking discussions on the streets instead of Parliament, defaming the Election Commission and tarnishing India's image abroad. Shah said the Congress leader should focus on understanding national issues rather than going on foreign vacations.Shah urged people to examine the original Constitution, saying its illustrations depicted India's civilisational and historical figures and events."To those who are opposing our civilisation, I want to tell them that if you have 10 to 15 minutes in your life for the Constitution, please look at the original copy of the Constitution once," he said.He listed illustrations depicting Lord Ram's arrival in Ayodhya, Lord Buddha, Lord Mahavira, Guru Gobind Singh, Rani Lakshmibai, the Dandi March and Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose.Shah defends Constitution Day observanceShah said the spirit of the Constitution had been neglected among India's youth after Independence, until Prime Minister Narendra Modi decided in 2015 to mark November 26 as Constitution Day across the country.He said the annual observance was intended to take the values of the Constitution to schools, colleges and citizens."Respecting the Constitution is a very important and proud responsibility for all of us Indians. However, it is unfortunate that after Independence, an attempt was made to treat the Constitution merely as a guidebook for running the government, and the process of instilling and strengthening its spirit among the country's adolescents, youth, and citizens was forgotten," Shah said.He added that after Modi became prime minister in 2014, he decided the following year that November 26 would be celebrated as Constitution Day."When Narendra Modi ji became the Prime Minister of this country in 2014, in 2015 he decided that every November 26 would be celebrated as Constitution Pride Day, so that the highest values of our Constitution could be carried to every school, college, and all citizens," he said.Shah also recalled the freedom struggle, describing it as a 90-year journey from 1857 to 1947, marked by sacrifices from people who gave up their homes, businesses, careers and education for the country's independence.He said the Constitution embodied the hopes and aspirations of those who had participated in the struggle and should not be viewed merely as a book."If we look at the Constitution merely as a book, we will never be able to understand it," he said.Shah promises UCC in BJP-ruled statesShah also spoke about the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), saying the Constitution's framers had included it in the Directive Principles of State Policy. He said every citizen, irrespective of religion, should have the right to live under a uniform law."Our Constitution framers included the UCC in our Directive Principles. Every single citizen in this country—irrespective of religion, whether Hindu, Sikh, Muslim, Christian, or Parsi must get the right to live under one uniform law. Laws should not be framed on the basis of religion, which your party, Rahul ji, outright rejects," he said.Shah added that BJP governments would move towards implementing the UCC in their respective states."Today I have come to state with clarity that in the coming days, wherever there are BJP-ruled governments, we are going to implement the UCC," he said.At the programme, Shah paid floral tributes to Dr BR Ambedkar and lit the ceremonial lamp alongside senior BJP leaders. Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta was also present. Shah, Gupta and other participants collectively read out the Preamble to the Constitution.Shah said the framers had placed power in the hands of the people, giving citizens the right to decide who would govern them while requiring those elected to exercise authority within constitutional limits.He said every word of the Preamble was intended to contribute to the building of a great India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Cost of living roadshow highlights support on offer
articles.summary: This event in Sheerness is funded by the Crisis and Resilience Fund for those facing cash issues.
articles.body:
A cost of living roadshow held in a Kent town is the "starting point" and "first step on the ladder" to resolve financial problems, a local councillor has said.

Organisations, including those which help people with health and wellbeing, managing bills and getting back into work, have been in Sheerness for the Swale Borough Council event on Thursday morning.

This event, funded by the Crisis and Resilience Fund which helps households facing financial crisis

Councillor Angela Harrison, deputy mayor of Swale, wants residents to know that "there is help support and guidance for you".

Among those in attendance was Nichola Hermitage from Positively Connected Kent, which helps people manage energy costs and fuel debt.

Reacting to the recent announcement that energy prices are due to go up by 26% in January, Hermitage said there were small measures people can take to mitigate the impact.

She said: "It's about 45p to have a ten minute electric shower; cut that down by in half and you know you can save."

Hermitage stressed that people should not "suffer alone" if they have built up energy debt, with help from the providers themselves and charities.

Connect To Work, a 12-month voluntary scheme designed to help people get back into work, offers "individual support" including with travel, clothing and job searching.

Alex Emery said the roadshow was "about being present in the community to meet people face-to-face for them to understand what we do".

The event comes as Save the Children has released new research into the rising cost of Christmas for families, centred around a survey of 2,000 people including 233 from the South East.

About two thirds of South East respondents expressed concern about being able to afford Christmas.

Harrison said: "It's about time we stopped trying to keep up with the Jones'.

"Christmas is actually about family. It's not about how much you can spend on your kids and the rest of your family."

articles.body:
Rock-duo Royal Blood are the latest act to be announced for a series of concerts at Ludlow Castle next summer.

They will appear on 24 July and will join acts including McFly, Becky Hill, UB40 ft. Ali Campbell, Paul Heaton and Courtneeners, with more yet to be announced.

Promoters Futuresound Group described Royal Blood as "one of the most important rock bands of their generation," who have played "sold-out headline shows and major festivals to audiences across the globe".

The Live at Ludlow concerts began in 2023 and have gradually grown, with 50,000 people attending over a series of weekends this summer.

Futuresound said Royal Blood would be featuring songs from their new album Dead Company, which was released earlier this month.

It follows the Brighton-based pair's 2023 album Back to the Water Below, which went straight in at number one on the UK Albums Chart - their fourth consecutive number-one album.

They will be supported next summer by Soft Play, Nova Twins and Bad Nerves.

This summer there were eight concerts held at Ludlow Castle, featuring Snow Patrol, Paul Weller, The Human League, Tom Grennan, The Streets, Rick Astley, Richard Ashcroft and Scissor Sisters, Corinne Bailey Rae, Miles Kane, The Lightning Seeds, Heather Small and others.

Recently, Futuresound were given permission to continue the events until at least 2023 and said they brought more than £1m into the town in 2025.

People in the Ludlow area will be able to buy tickets from 2 December, with the remaining tickets going on general sale from 4 December.

articles.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
articles.summary: Net migration figures of 77,000 in the year to the end of June mark the lowest this century outside of the Covid pandemic.
articles.body:
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.

Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boris Wave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.

As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.

The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.

As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.

Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."

A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

articles.title: Jordan Parliament debates ‘antiterror’ law after deadly Karak church attack
articles.summary: House votes to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law to its Legal Committee for review.
articles.body:
Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last month that killed nine people.

House of Representatives Speaker Ibrahim Tarawneh said the chamber had pledged to review legislation and consider amendments after the attack at the church in southern Jordan and the killing of a police officer in the capital, Amman.

The House voted to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law on Wednesday to its Legal Committee for review. The legislation will return to the chamber for debate and a vote before proceeding to the Senate and, if approved, royal ratification.

On October 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were wounded.

Last week, Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death for the attack.

On Wednesday, the court sentenced another man to death for killing the police officer in Amman. The officer was stabbed while on guard duty near the Sri Lankan embassy on November 5.

The government-backed amendments would raise minimum prison terms to 10 years and up to 15 years in certain cases while retaining the death penalty for the most serious offences, the state-run Jordan News Agency reported.

The proposed amendments drew criticism from First Deputy Speaker Ayatollah Freihat, who said legislation should not be based on knee-jerk reactions to events, FactJo, a Jordanian news agency, reported.

He raised concerns that the amendments could also harm freedom of expression in Jordan.

Freihat called on the government to withdraw the draft amendments and form a committee of legal experts to review the state’s criminal policy, criticising the use of “vague” formulations in defining “terrorism”, including “disrupting public order” and “harming the public interest”.

Earlier, King Abdullah II had said the kingdom would not be shaken by the attack on the church. Opening the new session of parliament this month, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

articles.title: The Witch Farm: The real Liz Rich reveals scariest thing she saw
articles.summary: Liz Rich reveals what it was like living in one of Britain's most haunted homes in south Wales in 1989.
articles.body:
The woman at the centre of a "real-life ghost story" that inspired a new TV drama says the scariest thing she saw was an "old lady" looking at her from her house.

Liz Rich moved from London to Bannau Brycheiniog, also known as Brecon Beacons , with her husband while pregnant in 1989 to a farmhouse now dubbed one of Britain's most haunted houses.

Within seven years Rich said their "idyllic, fairytale" home turned to hearing unexplained footsteps, seeing animals mysteriously die, apparitions - and an "old lady" who watched her from the house as she walked up the driveway.

Danny Robins, writer and creator of The Witch Farm , said: "It's one of the greatest ghost stories I've ever come across."

On Thursday Rich spoke to This Morning and said the scariest thing was: "I didn't like the old lady.

"The first time I saw her I was coming up the driveway with a push chair, and I glanced up at the play room window. It wasn't a nice room, it was on the top floor.

"I looked up and staring directly at me was this old woman, she was like a beige-grey colour. She was solid, wasn't see-through.

"She had a knitted cardigan and her hair was grey, but permed with the curly bits in it. I didn't like it."

The Witch Farm , a four-part drama by the BBC, explores the family's claims of poltergeist activity, of alleged possessions and even physical injury which affected them and the community.

Robins, who is best-known for his podcast Uncanny, said the idea for the new drama came after he made The Battersea Poltergeist podcast for the BBC, which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".

He said he was looking for a story "at least as exciting", adding "Liz really cut through".

He said: "I thought this was the big one."

Rich said different events that left them increasingly scared were "gradual".

"I have a mind that tries to look for logical explanations. If something goes bang, I think a light bulb blown," she said.

"The first thing I couldn't explain were footsteps which was like someone wearing hobnailed boots.

"Bang bang bang, on the wooden stairs. That really worried me.

"They were to become a common occurrence, maybe daily."

At one point, Rich said they had an electricity bill so high it was "impossible" and as if "it was for a factory".

She said the house's electricity meter span was out of control and later landed them a bill of £750 for three months, which is the equivalent of about £2,000 in today's money.

This led the the couple to try an experiment.

"If you turn all the electrical appliances off in the house the little wheel would still keep going on, and then stop and pick up speed.

"We had experts and the electric board in, and they couldn't explain it. Eventually we got in a solicitor to help."

Robins said the series was about "real people who went through hell" adding Rich was "still scared after all these years".

"Liz's story stumbled into my lap, basically.

"It was that thing I rarely feel, a sense of tingles down my spine. Sitting opposite somebody and you get that sense of fear from them, you see the whites of their eyes light up and you feel a little tremble in their voice."

He said he was "torn" about whether he believed in ghosts.

"I've never had my own experience, I've never witnessed something myself.

"I can't fully sign up for team believer, but I can't explain the stories I'm told and it chips away at you."

Rich said the family who has lived there for nearly 30 years have had "no problems" but the people living before her and Bill did.

The Witch Farm is available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales
